Proximal Humerus Fractures
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Often occur about the physis or metaphysis
Most often observed in older children and adolescents
Toddlers sustain buckle-type fractures
Tremendous healing potential with little functional impairment
Epidemiology
Less than 5% of fractures in children

Epidemiology
Proximal humeral fractures are relatively uncommon injuries, representing less than 5%
of all childhood fractures.1,2 Because of the well-vascularized periosteum and closeness
to the physis, such fractures have excellent healing and remodeling potential. In
addition, because of the near universal motion about the glenohumeral joint, little
functional impairment may be observed. Therefore, most proximal humeral fractures
can be appropriately managed nonsurgically (Resource 1; Videos 1 and 2).

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
The glenoid is a shallow fossa that articulates with the humeral head.
The radius of curvature of the humeral head is three times greater than the glenoid.
Lack of bony constraint permits substantial range of motion.
Proximal humerus growth
The proximal humeral epiphysis ossifies at approximately 6 months of age.
The greater tuberosity is a secondary ossification center that ossifies between ages 1 and 3
years.
The lesser tuberosity is a secondary ossification center that ossifies between ages 4 and 5
years.
The greater and lesser tuberosities coalesce between ages 5 and 7 years.
The proximal humerus epiphysis contributes to 80% of the longitudinal growth of the
humerus.
The proximal humerus physis closes between ages 14 and 17 years in girls and ages 16 and
18 years in boys.
Vascular Anatomy
An adult cadaver model study showed that the anterior and posterior humeral circumflex
arteries are the primary blood supply for the proximal humerus, with the posterior humeral
circumflex artery providing 64% of the blood supply to the humeral head and the anterior
circumflex artery providing 36% of the blood supply to the humeral head.3
Neural Anatomy
The axillary nerve is close to the proximal humerus and is most at risk for injury during
dislocations and proximal humerus fractures.
Tendons
The long head of the proximal biceps tendon runs in the bicipital groove of the proximal
humerus and is intracapsular.

Joints and Ligaments
A large portion of the proximal humeral physis is extracapsular and, therefore, is susceptible
to injury.
The glenohumeral joint relies primarily on soft-tissue structures for stability.
Cartilaginous labrum
Disruption of the anteroinferior labrum results in a Bankart lesion, which is associated with
traumatic anterior shoulder dislocations.
Glenohumeral ligaments: superior, middle, and inferior
The anteroinferior glenohumeral ligament contributes most to stability in abduction and
external rotation of the shoulder.
Musculature
Muscle insertions on the proximal humerus affect fracture patterns and displacement.
The subscapularis inserts on the lesser tuberosity.
The supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and teres minor insert on the greater tuberosity and
posterosuperior epiphysis.
The pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi insert on the anteromedial metaphysis.
Fractures proximal to the pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi insertions result in flexion,
external rotation, and abduction of the proximal fragment because of the pull of the
rotator cuff muscles.
The distal fragment is displaced proximally by the biceps and triceps and medially by the
pectoralis major latissimus dorsi and the teres major.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The proximal humeral epiphysis does not ossify until approximately 6 months of age. In
addition, the greater and lesser tuberosities have separate secondary centers of
ossification, which become visible at ages 1 to 3 years and 4 to 5 years, respectively. The
tuberosities come together between ages 5 and 7 years and then fuse to the rest of the
humeral head between ages 7 and 13 years. The proximal humeral physis contributes to
80% of the longitudinal growth of the humerus and closes at ages 14 to 16 years in girls
and ages 16 to 18 years in boys.4, 5

In addition to the epiphysis, the articular surface of the humeral head encompasses the
proximal medial corner of the metaphysis, making a portion of the metaphysis an intra-
articular structure; however, most of the proximal humeral physis is extracapsular, and,
therefore, most fractures of the proximal humerus involve the physis. The periosteum of
the proximal humerus is thick and strong along the posteromedial aspect. In patients
with a displaced fracture, interposed periosteum may block reduction.
The muscles inserting on the proximal humerus influence the fracture pattern and
displacement. Understanding these forces is critical for successful fracture reduction.
The subscapularis inserts on the lesser tuberosity, whereas the supraspinatus,
infraspinatus, and teres minor attach to the greater tuberosity and the posterosuperior
epiphysis. The deltoid tubercle lies along the lateral aspect of the humeral diaphysis. The
pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi muscles insert along the anteromedial aspect of
the metaphysis. In patients with a fracture proximal to the pectoralis major, the proximal
humerus is abducted, flexed, and externally rotated by the rotator cuff muscles, and the
diaphyseal portion is internally rotated and displaced proximally and medially. For
fractures distal to the deltoid insertion, the proximal fracture fragment is abducted by
the deltoid and flexed by the pectoralis major. An isolated fracture of the lesser
tuberosity may be displaced by the pull of the subscapularis (Figure 1).

The vascularity of the proximal humerus arises from the anterior and posterior humeral
circumflex arteries, which are branches of the axillary artery. The humeral head derives
most of its vascular supply from the ascending branch of the anterior humeral
circumflex artery.6
The axillary nerve is the closest and most at-risk nerve in proximal humerus fractures.
The axillary nerve arises from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus. It travels over the
anterior aspect of the subscapularis muscle and passes just inferior to the glenohumeral
joint. At this point, it enters the quadrilateral space bordered by the teres minor
superiorly, the teres major inferiorly, the long head of the triceps medially, and the
humerus laterally to innervate the deltoid and the teres minor. It also provides sensation
to the lateral aspect of the shoulder.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Birth-related: rotational and hyperextension forces during delivery
Risk factors: macrosomia, difficult delivery, breech
Traumatic: sports, motor vehicle collisions, falls
Forces that place the arm into nonphysiologic positions
Pathologic: unicameral or aneurysmal bone cysts, sarcomas
Neuropathic: Chiari malformation, syringomyelia
Nonaccidental trauma: infants and young children

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Proximal humerus fractures occur via several characteristic mechanisms of injury. Birth-
related fractures result from hyperextension and rotational forces during labor and
delivery. Risk factors include a difficult delivery, macrosomia, and/or breech
presentation.7,8 In older children, proximal humerus fractures typically result from
traumatic mechanisms of injury, including direct or indirect trauma. Indirect trauma may
result from falls or non-physiologic positioning.9
The proximal humerus also is a common area for pathologic fractures in children. Most
commonly, unicameral or aneurysmal bone cysts cause the pathologic fracture, but
malignant lesions also are possible.10 Neuropathic conditions, such as an Arnold-Chiari
malformation or syringomyelia also may result in pathologic fractures of the proximal
humerus.
Proximal humerus fractures also may result from nonaccidental trauma; therefore, a
careful assessment is crucial in infants and young children.11
Associated Injuries
Glenohumeral joint dislocations
Ipsilateral fractures of the upper limb
Brachial artery injury

Associated Injuries
The proximal humerus may have concomitant dislocations of the glenohumeral joint,
particularly with high-energy mechanisms of injury. Proximal humerus fractures also
may have concomitant intra-articular or apophyseal avulsion fractures. Optimal
radiographs and careful assessment are important. Ipsilateral fractures of the upper
limb also are possible. Proximal humerus fractures may be associated with
neurovascular injury, particularly to the axillary nerve. Radial nerve and total brachial
plexus injuries also are possible. These injuries typically are observed if the distal
diaphyseal segment displaces medially and proximally into the region of the brachial
plexus. Spontaneous neurologic recovery is observed in most patients within 9 to 12
months.12,13 Proximal humerus fractures associated with an arterial injury require
emergent reduction and stabilization in combination with vascular exploration and
repair. Additional injuries to the thorax, including rib fractures and/or a pneumothorax,
also have been reported.

Injury Classification
Physeal fractures are classified according to the Salter-Harris system. Proximal humerus
fractures through the metaphysis most commonly occur in children aged 5 to 12 years.
These fractures typically are described according to their radiographic findings.14
In addition, Neer and Horwitz9 proposed a classification system based on the amount of
fracture displacement (Table 1). In grade I fractures, up to 5 mm of displacement is
present. Grade II fractures are displaced up to one-third of the cortical diameter of the
humeral diaphysis. Grade III fractures are displaced up to two-thirds of the cortical
diameter of the humeral diaphysis. grade IV fractures are displaced more than two-
thirds of the cortical diameter of the humeral diaphysis.

Neurovascular Examination
In newborns, the signs and symptoms of a proximal humerus fracture often are subtle.
The most frequent symptom is irritability with handling of the affected extremity. In
addition, pseudoparalysis, in which a loss of movement of the extremity occurs, may be
indicative of a fracture. Septic arthritis and osteomyelitis must be ruled out in neonates.
In older children and adolescents, the diagnosis is more obvious. Patients present with
pain, swelling, ecchymosis, and/or limited range of motion, often with a history of a
traumatic injury. They typically hold the arm against the body in adduction and guard
against movement. Asymmetry in the contour of the shoulder girdle may be observed
compared with the uninjured side. Associated shoulder dislocations also must be ruled
out. In anterior dislocations, the acromion is prominent, the posterolateral shoulder is
flattened, and prominence may be observed anteriorly from the humeral head. In
posterior joint dislocations, the patient presents with internal rotation and has limited

The radiographic signs of a proximal humerus fracture in infants are subtle. They may
include asymmetric positioning of the proximal humeral metaphysis in relationship to
the scapula/acromion. Radiographs of the contralateral shoulder may be helpful. In
older children, plain radiographs will confirm the diagnosis. Orthogonal views are
necessary. AP and axillary views are obtained to evaluate for glenohumeral joint
dislocation and lesser tuberosity fractures. Obtaining axillary radiographs in the acutely
injured child may be difficult. Alternative views include a transthoracic scapula Y view or
Velpeau view.17 If necessary, CT or MRI may be performed in patients with a posterior
glenohumeral fracture-dislocation, intra-articular fracture, or occult fracture.

Nonsurgical Management
Most proximal humerus fractures can be managed nonsurgically because of their
remodeling potential and the compensatory motion afforded by the shoulder joint.
Neonatal proximal humerus fractures can be managed via simple pinning of the sleeve
to the garment, with the use of Webril padding/stockinette, or via swathe immobilization.

Closed reduction, serial radiographs, or advanced imaging studies rarely is necessary in
infants, in whom healing is rapid and typically occurs within 2 to 3 weeks, and little
concern is necessary for functional limitations.18
Nondisplaced or minimally displaced fractures in older children and adolescents also
may be managed with the use of a simple sling and swathe or a shoulder immobilizer
(Figure 4). Late fracture displacement is uncommon; therefore, serial radiographic
evaluations are unnecessary, and patients have excellent long-term results. Similarly,
stress fractures of the proximal humerus are amenable to management via rest, activity
modifications, and/or simple sling immobilization.19

additional controversy. In general, fracture reduction and immobilization are
recommended for Neer-Horwitz grade III and grade IV injuries with unacceptable
alignment.19 Numerous reduction maneuvers have been described, all of which aim to
reverse the deformity and counteract the deforming forces. Closed reduction can be
performed by applying longitudinal traction to the distal brachium, followed by
abduction, flexion, and external rotation. Initial adduction and internal rotation may be
necessary to relax the pectoralis major. In physeal fractures, manipulation with the
assistance of conscious sedation or general anesthesia should be considered to limit
potential injury to the physis. After reduction, fracture stability should be assessed;
however, recent prospective data suggest that, in adolescents with a displaced fracture
managed nonsurgically, closed reduction under sedation does not substantially improve
radiographic alignment or functional outcomes compared with immobilization without
reduction, calling into question the necessity of reduction in this patient group.20
Interposed soft tissue at the fracture site, such as the periosteum, capsule, and/or long
head of the biceps tendon, may prevent successful closed reduction. In these situations,
open reduction via a limited anterior deltopectoral approach may be necessary. Good
healing and functional return may be expected, even in patients in whom alignment is
improved to acceptable but not anatomic parameters. In older children who have
undergone acceptable closed reduction, loss of reduction after initial manipulation has
been reported to be as high as 50%. This finding suggests that internal fixation, typically
via percutaneous pinning with the use of smooth Steinmann pins, should be considered
in the treatment of older patients with a severely displaced injury. A recent prospective
study showed that, even with greater than 50% displacement and greater than 30° of
angulation, nonsurgical treatment resulted in similar patient-reported outcomes and
range of motion.21

Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative planning includes appropriate AP and lateral radiographs of the humerus
to assess fracture location, pattern, and displacement. Appropriate size implants should
be determined preoperatively. Dissimilar from the 4.5-mm plates used in adults, smaller
3.5-mm plates often are adequate for fractures in children and adolescents. In addition,
careful preoperative documentation of neurovascular status is important given the
known risks of traumatic and iatrogenic radial nerve injuries.
Patient positioning depends on the planned surgical approach. For anterior-based
approaches, the patient is placed in the supine position and the affected limb may be
placed on a radiolucent hand table. If a posterior surgical approach is planned, supine or
lateral positioning may be used, with the limb adducted across the body. The
fluoroscopy unit should come in from the head of the patient or the contralateral side.
Commonly used approaches are the anterior and posterior approaches. In the anterior
approach, proximally, the deltopectoral interval is used. The cephalic vein can be
retracted medially or laterally. After the interval is developed, the periosteum is readily
visible and can be incised lateral to the pectoralis major tendon and the long head of the
biceps tendon. The anterior humeral circumflex artery is identified and must be
coagulated. Distally, after the deep fascial of the arm is split, the biceps and brachialis
interval are identified. The biceps is retracted medially. The brachialis then can be split
longitudinally because it receives dual innervation from the radial and
musculocutaneous nerves. Although extensile proximally, this approach is not extensile
distally.
An extensile approach is the anterolateral approach, placed between the brachialis and
brachioradialis. This approach also facilitates radial nerve exploration. An incision is
made over the fracture and lateral to the biceps. The biceps is retracted medially, and
the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve is protected. The plane between the brachialis

The posterior approach provides access to the middle third and distal third of the
humeral shaft. A posterior midline incision is made, and dissection is carried down to the
level of the triceps fascia. The triceps tendon is split longitudinally in the midline and may
be extended proximally in the interval between the long and lateral heads of the triceps.

the lateral epicondyle in adults but varies in children based on the size of the patient.
This approach is not extensile, and more proximal exposure is limited by the course of
the radial nerve supplying the medial head. Care must be taken to slide the plate
beneath the nerve and avoid iatrogenic injury or kinking.
Intramedullary nailing of humeral shaft fractures allows for stable realignment via
indirect fracture reduction techniques and minimally invasive implant placement (Figure
12). Intramedullary implants may be inserted via a posterior approach, via a small
posterior incision, or via a triceps-splitting approach to the posterior humeral cortex.
Alternatively, nails can be placed via the lateral and/or medial columns of the distal
humerus. Small incisions are made over the distal lateral and/or medial columns, and
corticotomies are created at the site of nail entry proximal to the olecranon fossa to
facilitate implant passage. The posteromedial soft tissues—including the ulnar nerve—
must be protected if a medial entry point is chosen. Nails then may be passed into the
intramedullary canal in a retrograde fashion to the fracture site. The fracture can be
reduced, and the nails can be advanced into the proximal fragment. In general, two nails
are sufficient, given that they are of appropriate diameter and contoured to allow for
appropriate correction and control. If two nails are not sufficient, a bouquet technique
can be used to progressively fill the canal with multiple nails. Typically, these nails are
placed under fluoroscopic guidance; however, a recent study suggested that
ultrasonographic guided placement may be safe and substantially reduce radiation

Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Similar to the management of any fracture , numerous potential pitfalls may be
encountered during the management of humeral shaft fractures. Nonsurgical
management of distal humerus fractures may be a challenge given the limited amount
of distal humerus that may be incorporated into a fracture brace or splint. In such
situations, medial and lateral extensions of conventional fracture braces or a long arm
cast/posterior splint may be used. These fractures also have the tendency for varus
malalignment; therefore serial radiographs are important.
Pitfalls also are associated with surgical management, particularly of distal fractures.
Closed reduction and percutaneous pinning techniques used for supracondylar humerus
fractures may not provide adequate stability. Alternative treatment options include open
plating or intramedullary nailing via medial and lateral epicondyle entry sites.
During ORIF via a lateral or posterolateral approach, protecting the radial nerve is
critical. Identification of the posterior brachial cutaneous nerve and/or the characteristic
fat stripe along the lateral aspect of the triceps may help identify the radial nerve.40
During intramedullary fixation, lateral-entry–only nails may help prevent ulnar nerve
injury. In such instances, the nails should be contoured into a C shape and an S shape to
allow for divergence. In addition, starting the entry point above the olecranon fossa
allows the nails to lay flush against the metaphyseal flare.43

Radial nerve palsies, primary or secondary, commonly are observed in patients with a
humeral shaft fracture. These palsies often resolve spontaneously. If they do not,
surgical exploration may be warranted. Compartment syndrome is rare, but patients
with an ipsilateral upper extremity fracture or vascular injury have the highest risk.
Vascular injuries also are rare but require urgent evaluation and management.
Malunions that are functionally limiting are uncommon because as much as 30° of varus
and apex anterior angulation may be accepted with little functional consequence.
Nonunion also is rare and is observed in patients with excessive soft-tissue injury,
vascular insufficiency, segmental bone defects, and/or underlying bone abnormalities.
Hypertrophic nonunions are managed via ORIF. Atrophic nonunions require ORIF with
débridement of the pseudarthrosis. In patients with a pathologic fracture or systemic
bone abnormality—such as osteogenesis imperfecta—intramedullary implants are
preferred.
Outcomes
Results of nonsurgical and surgical management typically are excellent regardless of technique
used.
